title: The narrator in the margin
bodyMd:
In the invented novel The Unfinished Register, a clerk narrates the history of a small observatory in orderly chapters. Dates follow dates; instruments arrive, directors retire, and repairs are completed. At first the footnotes seem to reinforce this administrative precision. They identify receipts, explain abbreviations, and correct minor errors. Gradually, however, they begin to contradict the confident narrative above them. The typography encourages an initial hierarchy: a broad column carries the story, while smaller type appears to offer assistance from below. Readers accustomed to treating notes as optional may skip the earliest corrections and retain the unqualified account. The later contradictions make that reading habit consequential. What looked like supplementary material begins to govern the interpretation of the principal narrative. The novel thus makes the arrangement of evidence part of its argument. Authority is not only asserted by the clerk; it is also produced by the reader who decides which parts of the page deserve attention.

One chapter celebrates the installation of a new telescope as the achievement of a director. A note records that a technician had proposed the design years earlier. Another chapter describes the observatory as continuously open, while a note reproduces a caretaker's account of weeks when no staff were paid. The notes do not simply replace false statements with true ones. Several disagree with one another, and their sources sometimes have obvious interests of their own. The reader is denied the comfort of exchanging one authoritative voice for another.

Critics have called this arrangement an attack on historical knowledge. That description misses the distinction between questioning an account's completeness and denying that anything can be known. The novel gives readers enough evidence to reject particular claims: the uninterrupted staffing claim cannot survive the payroll gap and the caretaker's testimony together. What remains uncertain is how to assemble the surviving fragments into one comprehensive story. The uncertainty is disciplined by evidence, not freed from it.

The clerk himself changes as the book proceeds. Early notes are attributed to unnamed editors; later ones admit that he added them after finding documents he had once overlooked. His authority is not simply exposed as fraudulent. It becomes revisable. By the final chapter, the main text contains an explicit gap where earlier chapters would have supplied a smooth transition. The blank is not a confession that history is impossible. It is the visible result of learning when the available record does not warrant a sentence.
